chapter: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
title: Russell Procope and the John Kirby quartet
summary: Procope's hard tone did not suit Hodges-style lushness, and Bechet's soprano is mentioned.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: We haven't talked much about Russell, Russell Procope, he was there for quite awhile.
Yes, Russell was a permanent member of the band. Russell's fame, though, stems from the quartet--

John Kirby. Russell was terrific. I don't think he ever became greater in his capabilities and things than with that John Kirby quartet. And you can get some of those records today and they're beautifully put together. Beautiful instrumentations, beautiful arrangements, and beautifully played. That was really one of the famous groups of its day.
Well Russell wasn't given a great deal to do except just be part of the section, wasn't he. I mean he had an occasional solo?
No, I mean in Duke's band.
Oh, no, because in a way he was like

a foreigner, there again, you know, like I was telling you about going into CBS and having a different tonation and everything that didn't quite fit what the general musician had in there. Now Russell's tone was a bit hard and to match it against Johnny Hodges' lush tone, and the band leaned more towards the lush type of work. So he never --he soon was switched over to clarinette, mostly. And so he didn't get a just chance on either instrument, really.
Played soprano part of the time too?
Soprano? I don't remember him soprano. Johnny played soprano.
Did he? I never saw him.
Well they were trying to -- the soprano stems from way back, you know, what's the fellow that went to France?
Sidney Bechet was the soprano king and so it was just a case of shifting around and trying to get a desired effect that you wanted.
